source: Reddy (2026) Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (TraceRetain, ICML 2026)
finding: Bounded in-context memory of past episodes helps on held-out ALFWorld tasks, but the retention policies (success/age/frequency scoring, FIFO, unbounded) are not distinguishable. Single seed.
numbers: Held-out eval (50 tasks, gpt-5-mini): TR-CEM 49/50, TR-Linear 48/50, FIFO 48/50, unbounded 47/50, no memory 39/50. Wilson 95% CIs overlap for all memory policies (e.g. [90,100] vs [84,98]). Noisy-write stress (75% distractors): FIFO P@5 15.8% to 3.8%, TR-CEM 16.9% to 16.6%.
limits: Table 3 is one run per policy; the author says differences are within CIs. No spaced or SM-2 policy; no per-lesson analysis. Clean ALFWorld does not produce the memory pollution the method targets.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: retention scoring does not beat simple policies when the store is clean; the revisit-schedule question is still open. Floor: 50 tasks cannot separate 47 from 49.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
finding: Lessons that an LLM keeps rewriting into a memory bank first help, then fall, sometimes below no memory. Keeping raw episodes beats forced consolidation. The consolidation schedule changes results on the same trajectory pool.
numbers: GPT-5.4 failed 54% of ARC-AGI problems it solved without memory, after consolidating from ground-truth solutions. Episodic-retaining agents had about 2x the accuracy of forced-consolidation agents. ALFWorld Qwen3.5-27B: 19/48 no memory, 37/48 at stage 168, 24/48 at stage 169. WebShop AWM: 0.64 at 8 examples, 0.20 at 128 (equal to no memory). PropWorld Dynamic Cheatsheet .812 to .229. ScienceWorld: per-task 'Fresh' consolidation beat cumulative by 203 points; the cumulative store had about 5x over-generalized and 20x useless entries (LLM judge).
limits: Mostly single seed, one 50-task evaluation per cell; the author says the work may be incomplete. Abstract page and companion blog read; full tables not re-checked. v2 revised 29 Aug 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: yes, order and merge process matter, and the named mechanism is stripped applicability conditions. Supports storing each lesson with its trigger condition and keeping raw episodes.

source: Zhang (2026) blog page: Useful memories become faulty (companion to the arXiv paper)
finding: Same-pool comparison of consolidation schedules: Static-Group (abstract per task family once) best, Static-All shows cross-family confusion, Stream (incremental) worst.
numbers: ARC batch sizes 1, 8, 32 compared; ALFWorld Qwen3.5-4B 15/48 none, 35/48 stage 168, 29/48 stage 169; 9B 15, 36, 26.
limits: Blog summary of the arXiv paper; single seed; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 9: an incremental streaming update is the worst regime, so a schedule effect on lessons exists, but this tests consolidation timing, not revisit timing.

source: Struggle First, Prompt Later: How Task Complexity Shapes Learning with GenAI-Assisted Pretesting (2025)
finding: Students who attempted a problem before using ChatGPT scored higher on the final test than those who went straight to ChatGPT (Study 1); AI-assisted vs fixed pretesting did not differ (Study 2); on a harder task (Study 3) the AI-assisted group did better.
numbers: Study 1 (n=60 analysed): final test pretest 91.85 (SD 9.52) vs no-pretest 78.59 (SD 7.62), t(58)=5.979, p<.001, d=1.543; recall test no difference (71.03 vs 72.90, p=.562). Study 2 (n=78): FP 85.71 vs AP 83.56, p=.319. Study 3 (n=87): final-test F(1,85)=5.839, p=.018, partial eta2 .064; means 69.65 vs 76.87.
limits: Human students; same-week test with no real delay. Group counts inconsistent in Study 2; task-complexity moderation not tested directly. The learner is human, not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: human attempt-first beat help-first at large size (d about 1.5), but whether the same ordering helps an LLM at equal tokens is still untested.
